scope_note: The vty transport fault is left to 2.8-004 rather than repeated.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command must be entered before the key can be generated?

exhibit.content:
SW1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
% Please define a domain-name first.

SW1(config)#

The switch has been given the hostname SW1 and a username with a secret.
The vty lines are already set to transport input ssh.

options.text: ip ssh version 2, which selects the key format to generate
ip domain-name followed by the organisation's domain
crypto key zeroize rsa, to clear any partially built key
service password-encryption, so the key is stored protected

items.explanation: An RSA key pair is labelled with the device's fully qualified name, so IOS needs both a hostname and a domain name before it can build one, and the error names the missing half directly. Option A selects the protocol version, which is set after a key exists rather than before. Option C erases keys, and there is none to erase. Option D encrypts passwords in the configuration and has no bearing on key generation.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What should the version setting be changed to, and why?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
hostname R2
ip domain-name example.internal
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 1
!
username netadmin privilege 15 secret Wr3nch-Harbour-42
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
!

A security review has asked for the version setting to be revisited.

options.text: Change it to 2, which closes known weaknesses in the older protocol.
Leave it at 1, since version 2 requires a key of at least 4096 bits.
Remove the line, so the device negotiates whichever version the client offers.
Change it to 2, which is required before login local will be accepted.

items.explanation: Version 1 has structural weaknesses that version 2 was written to address, and a device with a 2048-bit key can run version 2 without any other change, so pinning to 2 is the correct outcome of the review. Option B invents a key length requirement. Option C leaves the device willing to fall back to version 1 whenever a client asks, which is the situation being closed. Option D ties the version to local authentication, which works under either.
